searches.purpose: Locate professional history, foundational participant work, a current scope definition, independent quantitative and qualitative syntheses, adverse-effect and ethics material, refugee-context evidence and contemporary institutional continuation while excluding arts-in-health, recreational art, art education, adult colouring and expressive-arts programmes unless a source explicitly identifies a professionally delivered visual art therapy component

items.title: Becoming a Profession: The History of Art Therapy in Britain 1940–82
items.rights_note: Publisher record and contents for Diane Waller's history of British art therapy professionalization from 1940 to 1982; the copyrighted book body is not cached or treated as read, and a British institutional history is not a universal origin story.

items.title: Introduction to Art Therapy
items.rights_note: Open Library record for Margaret Naumburg's participant text; the copyrighted book body is not cached or treated as read, and Naumburg's dynamically oriented approach is one early route rather than the definition of every later art-therapy model.

items.title: About Art Therapy
items.rights_note: AATA's current professional definition distinguishes art therapy within a psychotherapeutic relationship, delivered by trained art therapists, from art activities, colouring products and training by non-art therapists; it is a professional self-definition, not independent outcome evidence.

items.title: The Acceptability and Relative Benefits and Potential Harms of Art Therapy: Qualitative Systematic Review
items.rights_note: NIHR qualitative synthesis of service-user and provider perspectives for non-psychotic mental health disorders identifies acceptability limits and unresolved evoked feelings among potential harms; it is condition- and evidence-base-specific rather than a universal contraindication list.

items.title: Active Visual Art Therapy and Health Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.rights_note: CC BY synthesis of 69 randomized studies across heterogeneous populations and outcomes found benefits for some outcomes but 81% of analyzed outcomes showed no effect and overall study quality was low; exploratory pooled effects cannot be assigned to every diagnosis or art-therapy protocol.

items.title: Clinical Effectiveness of Art Therapy: Quantitative Systematic Review
items.rights_note: NIHR review of art therapy for non-psychotic mental health disorders reports a small and heterogeneous trial base and little adverse-event reporting; absence of reported adverse events is not evidence of absence, and results do not cover psychosis or all visual-art interventions.

items.title: Ethical Principles for Art Therapists
items.rights_note: AATA ethics document covers client welfare, competence, informed consent, confidentiality, storage and display of client artwork, boundaries and cultural responsibility; it is aspirational professional guidance rather than an adverse-event study or substitute for local law and licensing rules.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Empirical Evidence on Art Therapy With Traumatized Refugee Children and Youth
items.rights_note: Open review of refugee trauma studies judged the evidence insufficient under CEC standards and notes mixed intervention components and weak controls; forced-migration findings cannot establish broad cross-cultural efficacy or erase differences among refugee communities.

items.title: About the American Art Therapy Association
items.rights_note: Official page documents AATA's present membership, education, research, advocacy and professional-regulation functions; a United States association's continuation does not define worldwide regulation or validate particular interventions.
